e.etymology: A Germanic name brought to England by the Normans, from elements meaning ruler and army. Harold is built from the same two elements in reverse order.
namesakes: Walter Payton (Hall of Fame NFL running back)

assoc.t: Walter White of Breaking Bad

e.etymology: A variant of Brice, from the Late Latin name Bricius, possibly from a Gaulish word meaning speckled. Saint Brice was a 5th-century bishop of Tours.

assoc.t: Bryce Canyon National Park in Utah

e.meaning: from the alder grove (Norman); also an Irish surname
e.etymology: From a Norman surname, Old French del aunaie, from the alder grove. In Ireland it anglicizes O Dubhshlaine, a clan name whose first element is dubh, black.
A respelling of Riley with the -leigh ending. Riley is an English surname meaning rye clearing and also a form of the Irish surname Reilly.
From French Céleste, from Latin caelestis, heavenly, from caelum, sky.

assoc.t: Celeste, 2018 indie video game about climbing a mountain
Celeste Pizza for One frozen pizzas

e.etymology: From an Irish surname, O Cathalain, descendant of Cathalán, a pet form of the old Irish name Cathal. It can also anglicize the Gaelic Mac Callin.
A K spelling of Caleb, from Hebrew kelev, dog, perhaps for a dog's devotion to its master. In the Bible Caleb is one of the two faithful spies Moses sends into Canaan.
From Arabic muhammad, praised, the passive participle of hammada, to praise. As the name of the prophet of Islam it is among the most common names in the world.

assoc.t: the prophet and founder of Islam

e.etymology: From the English place name Kimberley, an Old English personal name plus leah, clearing. The South African diamond town, named for Lord Kimberley, put it in the news around 1900 and it became a first name.
namesakes: Kimberly Williams-Paisley (Father of the Bride actress)

assoc.t: Kimberly-Clark, maker of Kleenex and Huggies

e.etymology: A pet form of Grace, the virtue name from Latin gratia, with the -ie ending.
namesakes: Gracie Allen (comedian, partner of George Burns)

assoc.t: the Gracie family of Brazilian jiu-jitsu

e.etymology: Usually treated as a modern variant of Elora. Wiktionary records another account that takes it from a Bantu language of Botswana with the sense my dream. Álora is also a town in southern Spain.

e.meaning: handsome; also from Cináed, a name of Scottish kings
e.etymology: The English form of two Gaelic names: Cináed, borne by early kings of Scotland, and Cainnech, handsome, a saint's name that also gives the surname Mackenzie.

assoc.t: Kenneth Cole, shoe and fashion brand

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name meaning deep or hollow valley in Old English. J. D. Salinger gave it to Holden Caulfield, narrator of The Catcher in the Rye.

assoc.t: Holden Caulfield, narrator of The Catcher in the Rye

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English preost, priest, plus tun, settlement.
A spelling of Lily, the flower name taken up in the 19th century. It also serves as a pet form of Lillian and sometimes of Elizabeth.

assoc.t: Lilly Pulitzer bright floral resort wear
Eli Lilly, the drugmaker that goes by Lilly

e.meaning: son of Colin; in Ireland, descendant of Coileán
e.etymology: From a surname with two main sources: an English patronymic from Colin, a medieval pet form of Nicholas, and the Irish O Coileain. Its use as a girls' first name is recent and American.
namesakes: Suzanne Collins (author of The Hunger Games)

assoc.t: the Tom Collins cocktail and the Collins glass

e.etymology: From Arabic Layla, from the word for night. English speakers met it through 19th-century literature, including Byron's poems, and through the love story of Layla and Majnun.

assoc.t: Layla, the 1970 Eric Clapton song, spelled with a y

e.etymology: From Hebrew rahel, ewe. In Genesis Rachel is the beloved wife of Jacob and the mother of Joseph and Benjamin.

assoc.t: Rachel Green of Friends

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Ishmael, from Hebrew Yishmael, God will hear. In Genesis Ishmael is the first son of Abraham, and Islam honors him as a prophet.

First spread as a given name by the Western novelist Zane Grey, born Pearl Zane Gray; Zane was his mother's family surname, of unknown meaning. It is sometimes taken as a form of John or of Arabic Zayn.

assoc.t: Zane, the ice ninja in LEGO Ninjago

e.meaning: man of Attica, the region around Athens
e.etymology: From the Roman cognomen Atticus, the Athenian, from Greek Attikos. Its modern use comes from Atticus Finch, the principled lawyer in Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird.

assoc.t: Atticus Finch, lawyer hero of To Kill a Mockingbird

e.etymology: From French Élise and German Elise, short forms of Elisabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.
namesakes: Elise Stefanik (Republican politician from New York)

assoc.t: Für Elise, Beethoven's piano piece

e.etymology: The French form of Latin Camilla and Camillus, a Roman family name linked to camillus, a youth who served at religious ceremonies. In France it is given to both girls and boys.

assoc.t: hurricane that devastated the Gulf Coast in 1969

e.meaning: of Mary; also read as Maria plus Ana
e.etymology: A Latinized form of Marian, from Mary, often understood as Maria plus Ana. It is also the feminine of the Roman name Marianus, from Marius.

assoc.t: Mariana Trench, the deepest part of the ocean

e.etymology: From an English occupational surname for someone who looked after colts. It carries a frontier ring from John Colter, the Lewis and Clark expedition member who explored Yellowstone.
namesakes: John Colter (mountain man who explored Yellowstone)
Colter Shaw (lead character of the CBS series Tracker)

e.etymology: A modern variant of Cason, a surname turned first name, in the mold of Jason, Mason and Grayson.
From Hawaiian kai, sea, and lani, sky or heaven, often read as heavenly sea. It is a modern Hawaiian name that has spread across the mainland US.
From Hebrew Miryam, the name of the prophetess and sister of Moses in Exodus. Its meaning has been debated for centuries; it is the older form of the name Mary.
namesakes: Miriam (prophetess and sister of Moses in Exodus)

e.etymology: From a surname, a variant of Case, an occupational name for a maker of boxes and chests; German families named Kirch and Kirsch also adopted it in the US. Most people hear the word cash or think of Johnny Cash.

assoc.t: cash, money in bills and coins
Johnny Cash, country music legend

e.meaning: dark-haired (Irish Ciara) or bright, clear (Italian Chiara)
e.etymology: A variant of Keira and Ciara, feminine forms of Kieran, from Irish ciar, dark. It is also read as a phonetic spelling of Italian Chiara, bright or clear.

assoc.t: Simba's daughter in Disney's The Lion King II

e.etymology: From the Irish surname O Cathasaigh, descendant of Cathasach, a byname meaning watchful. Its use as a first name owes much to the folk-hero railroad engineer Casey Jones.
namesakes: Casey Kasem (radio host of American Top 40)
Casey Jones (railroad engineer of American folklore)

assoc.t: Casey at the Bat, the classic baseball poem
Casey's, Midwestern convenience store chain

e.etymology: A spelling of Jordan with a y, used mostly for girls. Jordan comes from the river of the Holy Land, Hebrew Yarden; in the Middle Ages it was given to children baptized with water crusaders brought home.

assoc.t: sounds the same as Jordan: Michael Jordan and Air Jordans
sounds the same as Jordan, the Middle Eastern country
